items.title: The Great Storm of October 1987
items.summary: A deep Atlantic depression crossed southern England during the night of 15–16 October 1987, bringing destructive winds to England and northern France. The Met Office counts 18 deaths directly caused by the storm in England. About 15 million trees were blown down, and at the peak 3 million homes and businesses were without electricity. Gusts reached 98 knots at Shoreham-by-Sea and at least 216 km/h on the Normandy coast.

impacts.text: The Met Office counts 18 direct storm deaths in England. This excludes deaths in other countries.

The Forestry Commission estimated 15 million fallen trees, representing 3.9 million cubic metres of timber. It reported 3 million householders and businesses without electricity at the peak of the cuts, and no Southern Region trains running on the morning of 16 October.
Buildings and boats were damaged. Fallen trees blocked transport and broke power lines. Gatwick Airport closed.

history.text: Later forecasts shifted the main threat south. Evening broadcasts emphasised rain and missed the exceptional winds. Michael Fish denied that a hurricane was coming; the Met Office says he meant another Atlantic system.
Emergency authorities received warnings, and the Ministry of Defence was alerted at 0135 UTC on 16 October.

Afterwards, more ocean buoys were deployed to watch the seas south-west of the British Isles, and the Met Office set up the National Severe Weather Warning Service to warn emergency services and the public.

why_interesting.text: The low deepened by 17 hPa in 12 hours as it crossed the Bay of Biscay. The pressure rises behind it were exceptional: 12 hPa in one hour at Hurn, near Bournemouth.
Its track took it from west of Spain to north-west of Brittany by 00 GMT 16 Oct, over Exeter at 02 GMT and to Hull around 05–06 GMT. The most damaging winds lay south and south-east of the track.
It became a key case for the sting jet: air descending from the cloud head near its hooked tip, bringing the damaging winds seen in the dry slot.
Some records were revised. The Met Office later reduced Gorleston's 106 knots to 85 knots because the anemometer cups were bent, leaving Shoreham as the strongest measured gust in England.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 reaches 951 hPa off Brittany at 22 UTC 15 Oct, close to published central-pressure analyses of 952–953 hPa around 00 GMT 16 Oct. Its peak gusts at Shoreham are 40 m/s during 03–04 UTC 16 Oct and at Pointe du Roc 35 m/s during 00–01 UTC 16 Oct, below the station evidence. The largest shortfall is at Pointe du Roc, where the recorder reached 60 m/s, so the actual peak remains uncertain. These differences likely reflect the coarse representation of coastlines, exposed headlands and small wind features; London’s rooftop instrument also differs from a standard surface wind measurement.

items.title: Cyclone Gabrielle

where.label: North Island, especially Tairāwhiti and Hawke's Bay

items.summary: Gabrielle passed close to the North Island on 12–14 February 2023 NZDT as an ex-tropical cyclone. Northland, Auckland and the Coromandel were affected first, followed by severe flooding and slips in Tairāwhiti and Hawke's Bay overnight on 13–14 February. In March 2023, New Zealand Police counted 11 deaths in circumstances related to the cyclone, and Mokohīnau recorded a gust of 150 km/h. In Hawke's Bay, flooding breached 5.3 km of stopbanks and washed away six major road bridges and a rail bridge.

impacts.text: New Zealand Police reported 11 deaths in circumstances related to Cyclone Gabrielle on 7 March 2023. This is their cyclone-related count, without a direct/indirect split.

Floods and slips cut roads across the north and east. At Te Karaka, inland of Gisborne, flooding of the Waipāoa River left about 500 people on a hill for 27 hours on 14 February NZDT. Orchards, vineyards and farmland in Hawke's Bay were flooded and covered in silt.

In Hawke's Bay, 5.3 km of stopbanks were breached, and six major road bridges and a rail bridge were washed away. Flooding of Redclyffe Substation disrupted electricity supplies to Napier and parts of Hastings.

The independent flood review recorded almost 1,700 Hawke's Bay properties with damage assessment stickers. It reported 287 properties classified as unsafe for continued residential use under the voluntary buy-out scheme. Marae, homes and burial grounds were severely affected.

PERILS estimated New Zealand insured property losses at NZ$2.174 billion in its final assessment of 16 February 2024; the price year was not stated. This covers residential and commercial property insurance, including business interruption where available, rather than total economic damage.

history.text: MetService began heavy rain and strong wind watches on 9 February. Orange warnings followed on 11 February, with the first red warnings that afternoon. Red rain warnings ultimately covered Northland, Auckland, Coromandel, Gisborne and Hawke's Bay.

Newstalk ZB reported Gabrielle's approach on 12 February. The Broadcasting Standards Authority later recorded that MetService's public messaging continued to stress extreme impacts after the system lost its tropical classification.

By the July 2024 flood review, repairs included reinstatement of 35 damaged rain and river monitoring sites. The review recommended more resilient communications, better flood forecasting and clearer evacuation triggers.

The 2024 government inquiry into the North Island severe weather events found that preparedness, communications and warnings had been inadequate in some places. It called for changes to emergency management design, funding and operations, recognising the value of community preparation and response.

why_interesting.text: Losing its tropical classification did not end Gabrielle's development. Interaction with the subtropical jet and a disturbance arriving from the Tasman Sea helped it strengthen again. Its centre slowed near Great Barrier Island and the Coromandel overnight on 13–14 February NZDT, then moved towards East Cape.
The storm's size spread damaging weather across many regions together. Already wet ground increased the effects of rain and wind, while storm surge and onshore winds impeded river outflow to the sea.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 shows pressure falling across Auckland and a slow centre near Great Barrier Island during 12–17 UTC 13 Feb, reaching about 967 hPa at 15 UTC 13 Feb. At Mokohīnau it gives a peak gust of 30 m/s at 03 UTC 12 Feb for that NZDT day, below the measured 150 km/h (42 m/s). Napier Airport receives 144 mm during 20 UTC 12 Feb–20 UTC 13 Feb, against 175.8 mm measured; Auckland Airport's peak gust is higher in ERA5 than reported. The quarter-degree grid smooths small islands, hills and coastal exposure, so local extremes and flood depths cannot be read directly from these maps.
